question: A healthcare worker sustains a needlestick injury from an HIV-positive patient. What is the MAXIMUM time window within which post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) must be started to be effective?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. PEP must be initiated within 72 hours of exposure — the sooner the better (ideally within 2 hours). The standard regimen is TDF + 3TC (or FTC) + dolutegravir for 28 days. PEP started after 72 hours is considered ineffective. Needlestick HIV transmission risk is approximately 0.3% per exposure.

Incorrect. While earlier initiation is better (ideally within 2 hours), the maximum effective window for PEP is 72 hours, not 24 hours. Starting within 24 hours is optimal but not the outer limit. The standard regimen is TDF + 3TC + dolutegravir for 28 days.

Incorrect. PEP initiated after 72 hours is considered too late to be effective. By 1 week, the virus has likely established a stable proviral reservoir through integration into host cell chromosomes — antiretrovirals cannot reverse this.

answers.text: There is no time limit — PEP can be started at any point after exposure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. PEP has a strict 72-hour window. The antiretroviral drugs work by blocking viral replication before a stable proviral reservoir is established. After 72 hours, integration into host DNA is likely complete and PEP cannot reverse established infection.

overallFeedback.feedback: PEP must be started within 72 hours of HIV exposure. Standard regimen: TDF + 3TC (or FTC) + dolutegravir for 28 days. Ideally start within 2 hours. Needlestick transmission risk ≈ 0.3%. After 72 hours, PEP is not considered effective.
Correct! PEP must begin within 72 hours (sooner is better). Regimen: TDF + 3TC + dolutegravir × 28 days. Follow-up testing at 6 weeks, 3 months, and 6 months post-exposure.
